newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Cameroon telecoms deal with France suspended.
newsitem.headline: Cameroon telecoms deal with France suspended.

text.p: A debt-for-equity deal giving France Telecom a stake in Cameroon's state telephone company Intelcam in advance of privatisation has been suspended, according to official Cameroonian and Intelcam sources.

Sources close to the Posts and Telecommunications ministry and within Intelcam told Reuters at the weekend that the state remained the sole shareholder and the overiding desire was for transparency in the eventual sale of the company.
"This (debt-for-equity) protocol has been suspended," one source close to the ministry told Reuters.

"Intelcam's board met on September 17... and there was nothing on the agenda about co-opting an administrator who was not a representative of the state of Cameroon which remains the sole shareholder," a senior Intelcam source said.

Cameroon signed the protocol with France Telecom on June 12. The then Secretary General at the Presidency, Titus Edzoa, negotiated and signed the deal, which raised nationalist hackles and caused waves within the ruling coalition.

Critics, foremost among them Posts and Telecommunications Minister of State Dakole Daissala, said the deal could compromise plans to privatise Intelcam, which as elsewhere in Africa is likely to interest U.S. and other foreign companies.
The World Bank, which is pressing Cameroon to privatise as a way of reinvigorating what was once one of Central Africa's most vibrant economies, expressed misgivings about the deal.
Opposition legislators denounced it as a scandal.
Officials at the time said that because of the $80 million debt Cameroon risked being cut off from the world during the Organisation of African Unity summit, which it hosted in July.

But critics suggested that the deal, which would have put former colonial power France in a strong position ahead of the sale of all or part of the state's stake Intelcam, called into question the whole privatisation process.

"This affair bears all the hallmarks of those who run Cameroon as if it were their own family property," Dzongang Albert, a member of President Paul Biya's party and the rapporteur of the finance commission, commented.

Daissala, who was bypassed in the negotiations and denounced what he called the "cut-price sale of Cameroon", issued a statement distancing himself from the deal, precise details of which -- such as the size of the stake -- were not released.

France Telecom is likely to remain a front-runner in any privatisation deal, initially targeted for the first half of 1997. France maintains close links with its former colonies and is a champion of Third World causes on the world stage.
